It's not like quantum computing being able to potentially compromise current standards in encryption is a secret, or even an open secret. As this grows to become a real issue, we'll simply move on. Basic reliable encryption is required for everything. For instance every time you log into your bank account you're basically screaming your login credentials out loud at the top of your lungs. It's not like you create a secret connection that only you and the bank can see or hear - potentially millions of people can. The thing that makes it secure is anybody listening would hear arb bliargh ghar arv arf arf and the bank responding in kind. And the nonsensical language changes every time you connect.

As for database stuff we can already search sorted databases in logarithmic time. In other words the time to search a database of 'x' entries is comparable to the equation 2y = x where y is a relative time requirement. So if you have a database of 256 entries it would take you 8 units of time. If you have a database of 4,294,967,296 entries it'd take you just 4 times as long or 32 units of time to search. If you have a database with more entries than atoms in the observable universe it'd take you 183 units of time. The bottle neck on databases isn't computational power, but access times and particularly access times for huge amounts of storage. That amount of storage is generally stored on disk, and disk access is incredibly slow. This video mentions square root of search space for searches. That is vastly slower than what we already have so I assume that's for unsorted searches, yet sorting is hardly a burden when you have effectively unlimited space as the NSA does.

In any case in my opinion there is a very real chance that the NSA's vast stores of information are handicapping them more than helping them. There is absolutely a thing as too much information. If you have a large enough sample you can find connections and patterns in just about everything, even when no such patterns actually exist. So for instance we know that pi is a non repeating sequence of numbers, yet we also know that there are a strictly finite number of combinations of x digits. So for instance most sequences of 100 characters of pi will eventually repeat. At a first level naive datamining of the information of pi one could easily interpret this to mean something it doesn't. Similarly with information on humans and metadata. You'll undoubtedly find connections, links, patterns and implications - even when none actually exist. It could very well happen that the eldest great uncle of every terrorist has gone to a school where the third letter of the school's name was an e. This doesn't mean you should start looking more carefully at people who have an eldest great uncle who's gone to a school where the third letter of the school is an e. That's self evident, but it's not so self evident when you start finding connections that aren't so obviously coincidental. The conspiracy theorists would argue that the NSA doesn't try to stop terror, but I think Hanlon's Razor is far more apt - Never assume bad intentions when assuming stupidity is enough. Ok, since nobody seems to have brought this up yet...

Quantum computers are good at certain problems. Most modern encryption (like RSA) counts on the idea that, to decrypt your data, it is easy to do the math when you know the numbers (your 'key'), but it's hard to do math to discover those numbers.

Most modern encryption counts on prime factorization as the central "hard problem". It can be stated as, "once I have multiplied two prime numbers together, it is difficult to discover what two primes I used, because factoring is guess-and-check".

Quantum computers have a very specific advantage in factoring prime numbers. But, that's not the only "hard problem" in mathematics. So, we can just make standards that use other hard problems than prime factorization, and we should be ok.
